definition: The total number of unique tokens a language model's tokenizer can represent.
details: Vocabulary size involves a tradeoff: larger vocabularies can represent text more compactly (fewer tokens per sentence) but increase the size of the model's embedding and output layers.

explainer.lead: Vocabulary size is the total number of unique tokens a tokenizer can represent, and it matters because it trades compactness against model size.

tiers.eli5: It's like choosing how many distinct words go in a dictionary: a bigger dictionary means shorter spell-outs but a heavier book.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers tune it to balance tokens per sentence against embedding and output layer cost; a pitfall is that a larger vocabulary inflates those layers.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally it is the cardinality of the tokenizer's token set; larger vocabularies yield fewer tokens per sentence but grow the embedding and output layers.

explainer.example: A 50,000-token vocabulary encodes a sentence in fewer tokens than a 10,000-token one, but its embedding matrix has five times as many rows.
